items.t: Siemens stock: Buyback pause highlights Healthineers spin-off
sum: Siemens announced on Monday, November 23, that it was suspending its current share buyback while preparing the planned spin-off of a stake in Siemens Healthineers. The company said the program would be interrupted from November 20, according to its share buyback disclosure.

Siemens intends to resume the suspended buyback after the spin-off. Until completion, technical repurchases are planned to keep the number of treasury shares constant while offsetting transfers linked to share-based compensation and employee programs.
The disclosure reported 357,791 shares bought back between November 16 and November 20. Cumulative purchases under the program reached 6,655,658 shares from its July 1 start through November 20.

Siemens stock last traded at 254.58 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 12:10 CET on Saturday, November 28, 2026, 0.78 percent above the Xetra close of Friday, November 27. On the week, the Xetra close fell 0.81 percent from 254.65 euros on Friday, November 20, to 252.60 euros on Friday, November 27.

The buyback pause links capital allocation to the planned separation of Siemens Healthineers. For investors, the next milestones are the formal spin-off process and the shareholder decisions required before completion.

The Siemens disclosure says the company plans to conduct the technical repurchase until the spin-off is completed and then resume the broader program. The timing makes the treatment of treasury shares a relevant factor in assessing capital returns over the coming months.

Operating profit increased 57.3% to ₹2,218 crore, while the EBIT margin improved to 21.7% from 18%. The company reported annual new orders worth ₹14,579 crore, representing 11.2% year-on-year growth.

sum: Siemens shares came under pressure as a broad selloff swept European technology names, with the stock down 2.5% at €258.25 in the latest session. Weakness on Wall Street and mounting doubts over whether the heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off weighed on the wider market, according to Cinco Días. A separate report put the day's decline at 2.6%, framing it as part of a tech-wide retreat triggered by questions over Nvidia's recovery — two readings of the same pullback that point to sentiment rather than anything specific to the Munich industrial group.

The market noise contrasts with a decidedly more constructive corporate picture. On November 12, Siemens raised its medium-term growth ambitions, telling investors it expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% for fiscal 2027, alongside earnings per share before purchase price allocation of €10.20 to €10.80.

Those targets rest on a strong fiscal 2026. Comparable order intake climbed 25% to a record €108.2 billion, while comparable revenue advanced 8% to €83.4 billion. On preliminary figures, the group posted records across order intake, profit and free cash flow, and proposed a dividend of €5.50 per share.

Siemens moved to deepen its semiconductor toolset on November 17, announcing the acquisition of Breker Verification Systems. The purchase is aimed at broadening its offering for verifying System-on-Chip designs, and the company expects the transaction to close in December 2026.

In the Netherlands, grid operator Enexis chose Siemens' fluorine-free switching technology on November 19. Standardized substations are set to lift capacity from roughly 10 to about 100 stations a year, with Enexis planning as many as 800 new stations over eight years.

Brokerage houses have been fine-tuning their views. Deutsche Bank lifted its price target to €275 from €270 on November 20 while keeping a Hold rating. items.t: Siemens Energy Shareholders Weigh Buyback Haul Against the Harder Test of Margins
sum: Siemens Energy's stock jumped 9.7% on Monday, a move that dpa-AFX linked to the return of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang to the helm of the AI chipmaker and the broader recovery in AI-related equities that followed. Timo Emden, an analyst at Captrader, said he considers it plausible that Huang's comeback bolsters confidence in the AI sector.

The rally coincided with fresh disclosures on the company's share buyback. Between November 16 and November 22 inclusive, Siemens Energy repurchased 1,497,117 of its own shares — roughly 1.5 million — and that transaction is now complete. Since the program began on September 24, the group has bought back approximately 10.3 million own shares, a figure covering purchases through yesterday.

For investors, the two developments raise a question that the headlines blur together: what exactly justifies a higher valuation? Buybacks speak to how Siemens Energy deploys its capital. Whether the company earns more from its business over time is a separate matter, one that must show up in earnings — and the yardstick there is the company's own margin target.

Siemens Energy is aiming for a margin of 20% to 22% by 2030, a set of medium-term goals it presented on November 11. What matters for shareholders is the path to that level. A convincing trajectory would see higher revenue repeatedly paired with higher earnings, with the improvement flowing through to the margin. Strong sales alone say nothing about profitability.

The fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 offers a reference point. Siemens Energy reported record revenue for the period, while adjusted earnings before special items more than tripled year on year. For the full fiscal year, revenue came in at EUR 44.2 billion, up 15.5% on a comparable basis. Orders rose 18.8% on the same basis, reaching EUR 68.1 billion, and the order backlog stood at EUR 164 billion.

Those figures, however, measure different things. The tripling describes growth against an earlier quarter; the 20% to 22% target describes earnings as a share of revenue. The growth rate alone cannot tell investors how close Siemens Energy has come to its margin goal.
The bull case rests on revenue and adjusted earnings rising together in the coming reporting periods.

Siemens Pauses Buyback to Ready Healthineers Handout as Shares Jump 6%
sum: Siemens has put its share repurchase programme on hold as of Friday's close, a technical step toward carving out part of its stake in Siemens Healthineers. The stock reacted with a 6.0% advance to EUR 264.95.

The suspension is not a retreat from buybacks. A so-called technical repurchase will keep the number of Siemens shares outstanding steady until the spin-off closes, and the company intends to resume the regular programme once the transaction is complete. Since the scheme began on 1 July, Siemens has bought back 6,655,658 of its own shares, including roughly 358,000 in the trading week before the pause.

Under the plan, shareholders would receive one Healthineers share for every two Siemens shares they hold, with 34.1% of the medical-technology unit's stock to be spun off. The distribution ratio reflects what investors would get if the deal goes through. Completion is targeted for May 2027, though the shareholder meetings of both companies must first give their approval — and those votes are still outstanding.

Chief executive Roland Busch told dpa that Siemens could absorb acquisitions in the region of EUR 10 billion where synergies justify the outlay, adding that the risk grows along with a deal's size. He did not name any specific target. None of these potential purchases are baked into the guidance: for fiscal 2026/27, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11%, and over the medium term it projects top-line growth of 7% to 11%.
The financial headroom is visible in the fiscal 2026 figures. Free cash flow at group level reached EUR 12.1 billion, up from EUR 10.8 billion a year earlier, while industrial net debt declined.

Momentum in the underlying business was on display in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, when Siemens reported on 12 November that order intake jumped 58% to a quarterly record of EUR 34.8 billion. Revenue for the same period rose 11% to EUR 23.7 billion, and profit from the industrial business came in at EUR 3.9 billion.

Analysts, meanwhile, are nudging their targets higher without turning more bullish. Deutsche Bank Research lifted its price target on Friday to EUR 275.00 from EUR 270.00 while keeping its "Hold" rating.

Siemens Slumps With AI Complex as Analysts Diverge and Grid, Chip Deals Build
sum: Siemens shares shed 5.7% on Friday, caught in a broad selloff that hammered AI and technology names across the board. The retreat came even as the Munich industrial group kept stacking up orders and acquisitions, and as sell-side analysts moved in opposite directions on the stock.

The wider market's jitters had little to do with Siemens itself. German broadcaster Tagesschau pointed to uncertainty over the buildout of US data centers and mounting worries about Nvidia as the forces weighing on sentiment. A Reuters report noted that the IPO of Anthropic failed to restore confidence in the AI sector, prompting investors to trim their exposure to the theme.

Against that nervous tape, Oddo BHF's Delphine Brault cut Siemens to "Neutral" from "Outperform" on Wednesday, trimming her price target to EUR 302 from EUR 310. Citi's Martin Wilkie went the other way the same day, lifting his target to EUR 340 from EUR 335 while reaffirming his Buy rating. Deutsche Bank Research added its own adjustment on Friday, raising its target to EUR 275 from EUR 270 and keeping a "Hold" stance.

On the corporate side, Siemens agreed on Tuesday to acquire US-based Breker Verification Systems, a move aimed at broadening its offering for testing system-on-chip products. The transaction is expected to close in December. The deal was first reported on 17 November, with the completion date given as December 2026.
Siemens is also pushing its software further into the cloud. On Wednesday it announced that its Simcenter X platform will be made available through Microsoft Azure and the Microsoft Marketplace.

In infrastructure, Dutch network operator Enexis selected Siemens' fluorine-free switchgear for the expansion of the Netherlands' power grid. The plan calls for up to 800 new substations to be brought into service over eight years.
Siemens Mobility, meanwhile, is set to supply Amtrak's Northeast Corridor with eight train sets comprising 80 new passenger cars, alongside a modernization program for 18 ACS-64 locomotives.

sum: Siemens Energy shares closed Friday at €116.00, down 6.8%, as investors trimmed exposure to AI-related names following Anthropic's stock market debut. The pullback, reported by dpa-AFX and Reuters, hit European suppliers to data-centre power infrastructure particularly hard, with the region's equity markets heading toward their steepest weekly decline since March. Siemens Energy, which manufactures equipment for data-centre power supply, was caught squarely in the downdraft.

The selloff, however, tells only part of the story. The Munich-based turbine and grid-technology group has spent the past two weeks rolling out a string of announcements that paint a far more constructive picture — record full-year figures, a beefed-up capital return programme, a hydrogen milestone and fresh analyst attention.

For fiscal 2026, Siemens Energy posted revenue of €44.2 billion and earnings before special items of €5.49 billion. The final quarter alone delivered record revenue of €12.8 billion, with pre-special-items profit of €1.54 billion and order intake of €14.8 billion. By the close of the fiscal year, the company's order book had swelled to a record €164 billion — a backlog that gives unusually long visibility into future revenue.

On 10 November, the group announced a further share buyback of up to €9 billion, running through the end of fiscal 2030. That sits alongside an existing repurchase programme worth up to €6 billion. Under the current scheme, Siemens Energy bought back roughly 1.44 million of its own shares between 9 and 15 November inclusive. A day later, the company proposed a dividend of €2.30 per share.

Siemens Energy said on 16 November that HyCoFlex, a research project it coordinates, had demonstrated industrial combined heat and power generation running on 100% hydrogen. At the Saillat site, the facility produced electricity and process steam from renewable hydrogen. The SGT-400 gas turbine used in the trial operated across its entire load range on hydrogen, including during start-up, according to the company.

Two Wall Street heavyweights weighed in on 12 November. JPMorgan lifted its price target to €250 from €245 while reaffirming its buy rating. Bank of America, by contrast, cut its target to €220 from €250 — yet also stuck with a buy recommendation.

items.t: Siemens Looks Past AI-Driven Slide to Nuremberg as Analysts Split on the Recovery Case
sum: Siemens shares closed at 250.00 € on Friday, down 5.7%, as a global selloff in AI-related equities gathered pace. Reuters reported that investors trimmed AI exposure following Anthropic's disappointing market debut, with the selling spreading beyond pure technology names. The retreat sets up a sharper question for shareholders: whether the industrial group's pipeline of product launches and customer wins can carry the stock, or whether proof of actual deployment is needed first.

The next public test arrives on 24 November, when Siemens holds a press conference with Rainer Brehm at the SPS trade fair in Nuremberg. Running from 24 to 26 November, the event will host the first public showing of the company's new high-performance DC contactor, rated for up to 1,500 V and 600 A. For investors, the technical specifications matter less than whether Siemens names concrete applications for the device.

More telling than any product unveiling is the step from technology selection to customer deployment. On Thursday, Dutch grid operator Enexis chose Siemens' SF?-free NXPLUS C 24 blue GIS switchgear for its network expansion. Enexis plans to bring up to 800 new substations into service within eight years — a commitment that gives the market something firmer to work with than a trade-fair debut. The word "up to" still marks the ceiling of the rollout rather than its guaranteed scope, so progress on commissioning will say more about the project's weight than the headline figure alone.

The same distinction between announcement and execution applies elsewhere in the group. Siemens announced the TIA Portal V21.1 automation software on Thursday, with the download scheduled for the end of November 2026 and boxed delivery in December. Separately, the company agreed on 17 November to acquire US-based Breker Verification Systems, extending its offering for AI-assisted verification of system-on-chips; the deal is expected to close in December 2026, subject to customary conditions. Delivering on these timelines would demonstrate that product planning is translating into action — though whether customers actually adopt the new software is a separate matter.

items.t: Siemens Energy Lays Out 2030 Margin Ambition as Record 2026 Results Meet a One-Day Tech Selloff
sum: Siemens Energy used its 2026 results disclosure to sketch a far longer runway than the market had priced in. Alongside record figures for the fiscal year just ended, the turbine and grid-technology group set out targets stretching to the end of the decade — a horizon that reframes the stock as a multi-year compounder rather than a single-quarter trade.

The shares, however, had a rough Friday. Siemens Energy stock dropped 6.8% and closed at €116.00 as a broad retreat from technology names gathered pace. Dow Jones tied the slide to mounting concern that spending on artificial intelligence may cool, combined with a general flight from risk. Suppliers of energy infrastructure for data centres were among those caught in the downdraft.

Management's answer to the volatility came in the form of capital returns. On 11 November the company proposed a dividend of €2.30 per share and put forward an additional share buyback worth up to €9 billion. The repurchase programme is already running: Siemens Energy reported on Monday that it had bought back roughly 1.44 million of its own shares between 9 and 15 November.

The fiscal 2026 scorecard was strong on every line. Revenue reached €44.2 billion, while earnings before special items came in at just under €5.5 billion. Net profit exceeded €4.1 billion and order intake totalled €68.1 billion.

On a comparable basis, sales grew 15.5% over the year, the margin before special items landed at 12.4%, and free cash flow before tax amounted to €8.8 billion. The closing quarter alone brought in €14.8 billion of new orders against revenue of €12.8 billion. By the end of the fiscal year the order backlog stood at €164 billion.

For fiscal 2027, Siemens Energy is guiding to comparable revenue growth of 14% to 16% and net profit of around €5 billion. The ambition then stretches out to 2030, when the company is targeting average annual comparable sales growth of 12% to 14% and a margin before special items of 20% to 22%.

That margin goal is the number to watch. Hitting it would mean roughly doubling the profitability level recorded in 2026 — and it gives investors a concrete yardstick against which to measure a stock that, for one session at least, was moving in the opposite direction to its own results.

Within the space of three days, both Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan lifted their price targets while keeping "Overweight" ratings on the Munich-based power equipment maker.

A separate trading day brought a steeper 3.5% decline to EUR 120.06, with Reuters reporting that momentum behind AI-themed positioning is fading and overall market sentiment remains fragile.

The analysts' confidence rests on a set of figures Siemens Energy released on November 11 for fiscal 2026. Revenue came in at EUR 44.2 billion, with a margin before special items of 12.4%. Net profit exceeded EUR 4.1 billion, and order intake climbed 18.8% to EUR 68.1 billion. The order backlog hit a record EUR 164 billion.
Management is putting that cash to work. The company proposed a dividend of EUR 2.30 per share and unveiled additional share buybacks of up to EUR 9 billion through the end of fiscal 2030.

For fiscal 2027, Siemens Energy is targeting comparable revenue growth of 14% to 16%, alongside a margin before special items in the same 14% to 16% range. Net profit is pencilled in at roughly EUR 5 billion. The longer-range plan is more ambitious still: average annual revenue growth of 12% to 14% through 2030, with the margin before special items rising to 20% to 22% by then.

On the technology front, Siemens Energy said the HyCoFlex research project on Monday demonstrated its SGT-400 gas turbine running on 100% renewable hydrogen. The two parties agreed the build-out on Wednesday, and Siemens says standardised substations will lift construction capacity from roughly 10 to around 100 stations a year.

The announcement came just a day after Siemens and Kärnten Netz signed a six-year contract covering the digitalisation and expansion of grid capacity, with Siemens supplying its Gridscale X platform. The Dutch order nonetheless failed to lift the stock: Siemens shares slipped 0.9% on the day, having closed 0.6% lower at €265.05 in the previous session.

Analysts are also turning more cautious. Oddo BHF downgraded Siemens from "Outperform" to "Neutral" on Wednesday and trimmed its price target to €302 from €310. Citigroup moved the other way, reaffirming its buy rating and raising its target to €340 from €335.

The mixed analyst signals come against a backdrop of upgraded ambitions. On 12 November Siemens lifted its medium-term target for comparable revenue growth to 7–11%, up from the previous 6–9% range. Over the same horizon, the group now expects percentage growth in the double digits for earnings per share before PPA effects.
For fiscal 2027, Siemens projects comparable revenue growth of 9–11% and earnings per share before purchase price allocation effects of €10.20 to €10.80.

The order book tells a similar story. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, order intake jumped 58% to €34.8 billion, while revenue advanced 11% to €23.7 billion. Net income climbed 32% to €2.4 billion. Shareholders are to receive a proposed dividend of €5.50 per share.

Alongside its grid business, Siemens is expanding in software. On 10 November the company signed an agreement to acquire Lauterbach, a provider of debug and trace solutions for embedded software. sum: Siemens has fixed 2 December 2026 as the publication date for its annual financial report and group annual report, both to be issued in German and English. The pre-announcement, filed under securities trading law, carries no fresh earnings guidance — it simply puts a date on the deeper reading of a fiscal year whose headline profit number needs careful handling.

That number: net profit of EUR 9.5 billion for fiscal 2025/26, down from EUR 10.4 billion a year earlier. The comparison flatters the prior period, which contained a EUR 2.1 billion special gain from the sale of Innomotics. Strip that out and the picture changes — profit at the industrial business climbed 13% to EUR 13.3 billion, a far better gauge of operating momentum than the group bottom line.

Running alongside that industrial strength is the digital story investors are being asked to price. Siemens Digital Industries revenue rose 16% to EUR 10.9 billion in fiscal 2026, giving the growth strategy a measurable base. What that figure cannot do is attribute any share of the total to the individual AI products the company has been rolling out — a distinction that matters when judging the pipeline.

The most recent of those arrived on Monday: a workflow linking agentic AI with additive manufacturing, demonstrated on a robotic gripper built for a humanoid robot and aimed at adaptive product development and production. Earlier, on 10 November, Siemens unveiled the HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit, which pairs AI agents with physics-based simulation to automate verification work on electronic systems. Early availability for selected customers is slated for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Development expertise is being bought in as well. Siemens signed an agreement on 10 November to acquire Lauterbach, a provider of debug and trace solutions for embedded software and SoC architectures — another building block in the electronic-systems design chain.

Where the tooling is still at the demonstration stage, the grid business shows how digital technology can be anchored in a customer's day-to-day operations. On 9 November, Siemens closed a six-year contract with Kärnten Netz to deploy Gridscale X, a platform that uses a digital twin to forecast network bottlenecks, among other functions.

items.t: Siemens Energy Backs 2027 Guidance With Hydrogen Breakthrough as Brokers Split on Valuation
sum: Siemens Energy has confirmed that its SGT-400 gas turbine ran on 100% renewable hydrogen in the HyCoFlex project, a milestone the company says was achieved even at full load in an integrated combined heat and power plant producing up to 12 MW of electrical output. The disclosure lands alongside a pair of bullish but divergent broker notes and a set of growth targets that stretch out to the end of the decade.

On the valuation side, Bernstein Research reiterated its "Outperform" rating on the stock with a price target of 210 euros, weighing the possible implications of the US midterm elections for future data center projects. JPMorgan, for its part, confirmed an "Overweight" rating on 11 November and lifted its target to 250 euros from 245 — a mark that sits above Bernstein's. Shares closed the prior session at 125.50 euros, down 1.1%.

The company's fiscal 2026 results, published on 11 November, provide the backdrop for both calls. Siemens Energy posted record revenue of EUR 44.2 billion. Order intake climbed 18.8% on a comparable basis to EUR 68.1 billion, while the order backlog stood at EUR 164 billion at the close of the fiscal year. The margin before special items came in at 12.4%, and net income reached EUR 4.13 billion.

Management is putting real money behind the story. The board has proposed a dividend of EUR 2.30 per share for fiscal 2026 and has dangled additional share buybacks of up to EUR 9 billion through the end of fiscal 2030.

Guidance for fiscal 2027 points to further expansion: revenue growth of 14% to 16%, with the margin before special items expected in the same 14% to 16% range. Net profit is targeted at around EUR 5 billion, and free cash flow before taxes at roughly EUR 10 billion.

Beyond that, the medium-term ambitions run through fiscal 2030, when Siemens Energy is aiming for annual revenue growth of 12% to 14% and a margin before special items of 20% to 22%. Whether the hydrogen test and the record order book can carry the stock past the gap between the two broker targets is the question now facing investors.

items.t: Siemens Energy's €164 Billion Backlog Meets a €2.30 Dividend Test
sum: Siemens Energy closed fiscal 2026 with record results and a dividend proposal that puts hard cash in front of shareholders for the year — a useful counterweight to a stock story that has leaned heavily on data-centre electricity demand. The company said on 11 November that it will ask its annual general meeting to approve a payout of €2.30 per share.

The numbers behind that proposal are substantial. Revenue for the fiscal year reached €44.2 billion, up 15.5% on a comparable basis. The margin before special items more than doubled, landing at 12.4%.
Orders tell a similar story. The order backlog finished the year at a record €164 billion. In the final quarter, order intake rose 5.2% on a comparable basis to €14.8 billion.

Management is guiding for comparable revenue growth of 14% to 16% in 2027, with the margin before special items expected in the same 14% to 16% range. According to Reuters, the company ties part of that margin improvement to demand for gas turbines and grid equipment, with data-centre expansion playing a role.

That framing matters for how investors read the growth case. Siemens Energy is not simply a bet on how fast new server halls get built. Berenberg analyst Richard Dawson points to predictable and more profitable growth, highlighting both the gas turbine order book and the service potential through 2030. The service business, in other words, carries weight in the bullish case alongside new equipment demand.

Gael de-Bray of Deutsche Bank Research takes a different route to a similar destination, arguing the shares are undervalued given possible revenue and earnings gains beyond 2030. Dawson emphasises the dependability of the business and its service pipeline; de-Bray puts the longer-run revenue and profit opportunity at the centre. Both are analyst expectations, not guarantees.

High expectations cut both ways. Management's own guidance — 14% to 16% revenue growth and free cash flow of around €8 billion — sets the operating yardstick against which the optimistic valuations will be judged. A full order book and favourable broker notes do not settle every question about what the stock is worth.

sum: Siemens shares fell 2.9% on Monday, extending a retreat that began on Friday following the release of the industrial group's quarterly results. The decline comes even as Evercore ISI lifted its price target on the stock from EUR 315 to EUR 320, keeping its "In Line" rating unchanged.

Media reports attributed Friday's losses to profit-taking after the figures published the previous day — an interpretation tied to Friday's trading session rather than Monday's move. Thursday's numbers had initially driven the stock sharply higher.

At the heart of the results was a record order intake of €34.8 billion for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, alongside revenue that climbed 11% to €23.7 billion. Siemens presented the full-year figures and discussed them with analysts and journalists. The company also raised its medium-term revenue growth target corridor from 6–9% to 7–11%, a forward-looking ambition rather than a result already achieved.

The research community has not spoken with one voice. Vertical Research downgraded Siemens from "Buy" to "Hold" on Thursday, according to media reports, with a price target of €300. Evercore ISI moved the other way a day later, nudging its target up to EUR 320 while reaffirming its "In Line" stance — a higher mark that did not come with a change in investment verdict.

Siemens is planning to transfer its stake in Healthineers to shareholders in fiscal 2027, at a ratio of one Healthineers share for every two Siemens shares. The move would put the medical-technology shares directly into the hands of Siemens investors.

Elsewhere on the corporate front, Siemens signed an agreement on 10 November to acquire Lauterbach, a provider of debug and trace solutions for embedded software and SoC architectures. The transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

Siemens Mobility, meanwhile, wrapped up a procurement programme on Friday by handing over the last of 294 Desiro ML Cityjets to ÖBB. Earlier in the week, on Wednesday, the company unveiled a stainless-steel valve designed for cooling AI data centres.

sum: В пятницу компания Oddo BHF перевела акции Siemens Energy с нейтрального на «лучше рынка», сохранив целевую цену на уровне 175 евро. Повышение происходит одновременно со смешанным пересмотром целевых показателей конкурирующих брокеров, а акции завершают сессию на уровне 131,60 евро.

Раскол среди аналитиков поучителен. JPMorgan повысил целевой показатель до 250 евро с 245 евро в четверг, подтвердив при этом «избыточный вес». Аналитик Фил Буллер отметил сильные квартальные результаты и обнадеживающий тон отчета о прибылях и убытках и повысил прогноз операционной прибыли до 2029 финансового года на целых 21%. Goldman Sachs пошел другим путем в отношении цены, снизив целевую цену до 200 евро с 212 евро в пятницу, но сохранив рекомендацию «Покупать».

Фоном является компания, которая только что объявила об амбициозной прибыли от капитала. В среду Siemens Energy предложила дивиденды в размере 2,30 евро на акцию за 2026 финансовый год, что резко превышает 0,70 евро годом ранее. Руководство также объявило о выкупе акций на сумму до 9 миллиардов евро до конца 2030 финансового года.

Эти обязательства основаны на убедительных цифрах. Сопоставимая выручка выросла на 15,5% до 44,2 млрд евро в 2026 финансовом году, а заказы выросли на 18,8% до 68,1 млрд евро. Портфель заказов составил 164 миллиарда евро. Прибыль до учета особых статей составила 5,5 млрд евро.

Заглядывая в будущее, компания прогнозирует рост сопоставимой выручки на уровне 14–16% в 2027 финансовом году, при этом ожидается, что маржа до учета специальных статей будет в том же диапазоне от 14% до 16%. sum: Investing.com -- Siemens AG (ETR:SIEGn) shares climbed to an 11-week high on Thursday after the industrial group reported better-than-expected quarterly results and raised its medium-term growth targets, as strong demand for AI-related data centre equipment and rail contracts drove record orders.

Shares rose 4.44% to €289.30, after touching an intraday high of €291.45, their highest level since August 28. The stock outperformed Germany's benchmark DAX, which gained around 0.9% during the session.

Net income for the quarter ended September 30 rose to €2.43 billion from €1.84 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 11% to €23.68 billion, while profit at its Industrial Business climbed 22% to a record €3.90 billion. The industrial profit margin improved to 16.8% from 15.3%.
Orders surged 58% to a quarterly record €34.77 billion, lifting Siemens' book-to-bill ratio to 1.47 and its order backlog to €143 billion.

Growth was led by Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, reflecting sustained investment in electrification, digital infrastructure and rail transportation. Smart Infrastructure's revenue rose 16% to €7.24 billion, with order intake jumping 40%, supported by large data centre contract wins, particularly in the U.S. and Europe.

Digital Industries also delivered stronger results, with revenue up 11% and profit increasing 50%, driven primarily by operational improvements in automation. Mobility's orders more than quadrupled, supported by major German rail contracts, including a €2.4 billion high-speed train order.

Looking ahead, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% in fiscal 2027 and earnings per share before purchase price allocation accounting (EPS pre PPA) of €10.20 to €10.80. sum: Siemens Energy's latest buyback disclosure landed yesterday, and it does more than update a running share count. The company confirmed it repurchased 1,539,908 of its own shares in the 2–8 November window, its seventh interim notification since the programme began. Since the 24 September launch, cumulative purchases have reached 7,390,216 shares.

The stock, meanwhile, climbed 6.2% as equity markets broadly recovered. Media reports credited falling oil prices and the wider rally with supporting the DAX at the start of the week, with Siemens Energy singled out as a beneficiary of AI-related investment and among the day's gainers ahead of its annual results. The shares closed yesterday at €124.48.

With capital already flowing back to shareholders, the question weighing on investors ahead of the figures is whether expected cash generation can sustain those returns. Siemens Energy is targeting free cash flow before tax of around €8bn, alongside a profit goal of roughly €4bn — two figures that together sketch the financial capacity the group intends to reach.

That makes the inflow of funds the metric to watch. It links operating performance to the room available for capital returns, and the buyback case would rest on firmer ground if the cash flow target is met and the company can convincingly explain why its financial strength should hold beyond the reporting period.

On the operating side, full-year targets call for revenue growth of 14–16%, with the margin before special items at the upper end of a 10–12% range. Investors will want to see whether growth and profitability are pulling in the same direction to underpin the expected cash inflow. Announced targets alone won't earn a favourable verdict — delivery is what counts, and the more persuasively Siemens Energy ties business development to cash generation, the more credible the prospect of further returns becomes.

The bullish scenario leans on continued profit growth. Analysts forecast earnings per share of €6.30 for 2027, up from an estimated €4.48 for 2026 — projections that assume substantial further progress. Supporting that view, earnings estimates have been revised higher recently, rising 4.4% over the past 90 days, and Siemens Energy has beaten profit expectations in five of the last six quarters.

Comments on pricing and margins will carry particular weight at the next set of results. Hard evidence could help separate industry-wide caution from the company's own trajectory. General confidence about demand, by contrast, would not fully answer the concern about a margin ceiling.

FuelCell Energy (NASDAQ:FCEL) shares jumped 11% on Thursday morning after the company announced a strategic collaboration with Siemens to develop scalable fuel cell power solutions for distributed energy projects.

The partnership has been formalized through a memorandum of understanding that combines Siemens' electrical engineering expertise with FuelCell Energy's fuel cell technology to accelerate the deployment of commercial energy systems.
Under the agreement, Siemens will design and supply electrical balance of plant systems for fuel cell installations, helping support the rollout of commercial projects exceeding 100 megawatts.

The companies plan to work together across project engineering, systems integration and delivery, focusing on distributed energy solutions that combine fuel cells, battery energy storage, microgrid controls and medium-voltage electrical infrastructure.
The partnership will assess opportunities to scale these technologies while improving deployment timelines, lowering project costs and expanding commercial adoption.
FuelCell Energy develops, manufactures, operates and services fuel cell power plants used by data centres, industrial customers, utilities and other distributed generation operators.

sum: The narrative around Siemens Energy has shifted dramatically. For years, the company was defined by the troubles at its wind turbine subsidiary Gamesa. Now, with the Indian business posting explosive growth and the wind division finally back in the black, the conversation has moved from crisis management to strategic ambition — just as a key board meeting looms.

The numbers out of India are striking. In the quarter ending June 2026, the Indian subsidiary reported a 39.3 percent jump in revenue, while net profit surged 67.8 percent. The operating margin of 23.6 percent is particularly telling — it suggests Siemens Energy isn't just growing in the region, it's also wielding real pricing power. Order backlog there expanded by 16.4 percent.

The demand driver isn't hard to identify. AI data centers are consuming electricity at an unprecedented rate, and India's electrification push is accelerating in tandem. Together, these forces are filling Siemens Energy's order books at a pace that seemed unthinkable just two years ago.

Group-wide, the third quarter of fiscal 2026 delivered revenue of EUR 11.45 billion, up 17.47 percent year over year, with net profit landing at roughly EUR 1.19 billion. The standout detail: Siemens Gamesa posted an operating profit of EUR 56 million — the first positive quarterly result from the wind unit since 2022.

The order backlog climbed to a record EUR 162 billion, and management reaffirmed its full-year guidance, signaling an earnings margin before special items at the upper end of the 10 to 12 percent range.

These results land in a week that could reshape the company's future. Media reports indicate the supervisory board has scheduled a special meeting for August 25 to discuss a potential spin-off of the "Transformation of Industry" division — the steam turbine and compressor business employing around 17,000 people.

The meeting is currently framed as a consultation, not a decision point. That distinction matters for investors. A clear commitment to a spin-off would signal a focused push toward the higher-margin, growth-oriented segments — gas turbines, grid technology, and the now-profitable Gamesa. A delay or rejection would raise questions about whether management intends to stick with the current broad structure.

The stock market is not always rational. This is currently very evident in the uranium market. While the AI-energy boom is driving a nuclear power renaissance, uranium stocks are largely on the sidelines. Does this present a huge opportunity for investors? After all, in the US alone, uranium demand is more likely to rise than fall, and the country is already overwhelmingly dependent on imports. For example, in 2024, the import rate for yellowcake (uranium oxide) stood at around 81%.

American Atomics aims to help change this. In a conversation with Lyndsay Malchuk of the IIF, company founder Conor Lynch explained that geopolitical tensions and disruptions to key trade routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz, have exposed the vulnerability of the global energy supply. Not only the US, but also countries like Japan, France, and China rely heavily on nuclear energy. According to Lynch, this could significantly drive global demand for uranium in the coming years.

American Atomics is particularly optimistic about the development of the US uranium market. The US Department of Energy aims to increase domestic uranium production from the current level of around 2 million pounds to 20 million pounds annually by 2033. Even this target, according to Lynch, would not yet fully meet US demand, thereby creating significant opportunities for new producers and exploration companies. American Atomics sees itself as a potentially key component of a future national uranium supply.

At the heart of the strategy is the so-called Big Indian Project in Utah. Management points to historical geological data and previous drilling that could indicate the presence of extensive uranium deposits. According to the company's assessment, there could be a so-called "Mirror Deposit," which, in terms of scale, could rival historic mining sites in the region. Supply squeeze: Europe's offshore wind sector sees turbine prices jump 40-45% as manufacturer options shrink
sum: Europe's offshore wind expansion is running into a structural supply constraint where the turbine market is becoming increasingly concentrated. GE Vernova, Siemens Gamesa and Vestas have historically anchored Western offshore turbine supply, but with GE Vernova having paused new offshore wind orders following a series of technical and operational setbacks, Siemens Gamesa and Vestas now account for virtually all turbines available to European developers. Rystad Energy’s analysis of the offshore wind market outlines a sharp increase in per-megawatt (MW) costs, with turbine selling prices rising by between 40% and 45% since 2020, outpacing manufacturing cost increases of 20% to 25% over the same period.

This pricing pressure is most acute in the turbine's most complex components. The nacelle, which houses the generator, gearbox and power electronics that convert wind into electricity, sits at the center of current supply constraints, while similar pressures are emerging in blade manufacturing, driven by increasing turbine sizes, longer production cycles and the logistical demands of transporting and installing next-generation components.

The supply constraint is not evenly distributed across the turbine value chain. It is most pronounced in nacelles and blades, where supplier concentration is high and substitution is limited, while towers remain comparatively more flexible, with a broader supplier base and lower barriers to entry. As a result, the market is becoming increasingly constrained in its most critical components, shaping the overall balance between supply and demand.

Europe's offshore ambitions are real, and the pipeline reflects genuine political commitment. But the market has moved into structurally tight territory: high demand, limited supplier diversity and rising turbine complexity. That combination gives original equipment manufacturers (OEM) real pricing power and the ability to be selective about which projects get built.

sum: In an exchange filing released on April 20, Vedanta announced that each of its eligible shareholders will get one share of Vedanta Aluminium Metal (VAML), one share of Talwandi Sabo Power (TSPL), one share of Malco Energy and one share of Vedanta Iron and Steel, for every share held in Vedanta. This marks one of the biggest corporate restructurings in India’s metals and mining space, allowing shareholders to hold a direct stake in distinct sector-specific firms rather than a diversified conglomerate structure.

While the record date for the demerger has been announced, the dates when the four new companies will be listed on stock exchanges BSE and NSE haven’t yet been disclosed. It is important to note that the shares of Vedanta currently represent the joint value of all the five companies. However, from May 1 onwards, the share price will represent the value of Vedanta excluding the four new companies.

Hence, the eligible shareholders of the company will see a portion of their money in the four new companies from the record date to their listing dates facing a discovery lag as they won’t be able to trade them, while the share price of the original Vedanta adjusts to the demerger and reduces in value.

Siemens Energy, the power transmission and distribution (T&D) business that was demerged from Siemens, listed on the NSE at Rs 2,840 per share on June 19 last year. This came 73 days after the record date.

sum: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has taken the stock market by storm in recent years, driving solid growth for several companies involved in its development and distribution.

Not surprisingly, many AI stocks have created significant wealth for investors in recent years. From Nvidia (NVDA -4.63%) to Palantir Technologies, Broadcom, or Micron Technology, AI has minted multiple high-flying stocks. The good news is that AI adoption is poised to take off in the long run. sum: A Siemens Energy supervisory board member has backed the company with a personal outlay of roughly €100,000, even as the stock trades well below its 52-week high and a swirl of market noise — from SpaceX speculation to rising bond yields — keeps the shares under pressure.

Laurence Mulliez, who sits on the energy technology group's supervisory board, acquired 660 shares at €151.91 apiece in late August, a transaction disclosed to Germany's financial regulator BaFin as an insider trade. Board-level purchases of this kind are often read by investors as a signal of conviction, since they commit personal capital without any obligation to publicise the move.

The timing is notable. The buy came after the stock had already retreated meaningfully from its record high of €195.38. At the current price of around €144, the shares sit roughly 4.9 percent below their 200-day moving average of €151.37 — evidence that the medium-term uptrend has flattened, even if the twelve-month performance remains firmly positive.

The market's recent skittishness traces back to reports that SpaceX is weighing in-house production of gas turbine components, a prospect that briefly knocked the stock to €139.50 on Thursday before it recovered. Analysts have been quick to pour cold water on the idea, pointing out that gas turbines account for only about ten percent of Siemens Energy's group revenue — hardly a scale that makes an immediate competitive threat existential.

JPMorgan reaffirmed its "Overweight" rating with a €245 price target in early September, with analyst Phil Buller arguing that SpaceX's plans appear aimed at individual components rather than a full entry into gas turbine manufacturing. RBC trimmed its target from €210 to €200 in late August but kept an "Outperform" stance, framing the adjustment as a recalibration of earnings expectations rather than operational doubt. Jefferies also shaved its target, to €210, while stressing that weakness in the gas turbine business stems from extended supply chains, not softening demand.

sum: Siemens shares gained 3 per cent as analysts remained positive after the September quarter topline beat the street's estimates, even as profit fell
Shares of Siemens Ltd. rose over 3 per cent on Monday as analysts remained positive after the September quarter topline beat the street's estimates despite a profit decline.

The heavy electrical equipment maker's stock rose as much as 3.31 per cent during the day to ₹3,186.3 per share, the biggest intraday rise since October 6 this year. The stock pared gains to trade 2.3 per cent higher at ₹3,156 apiece, compared to a 0.23 per cent advance in Nifty 50 as of 10:00 AM.

Shares of the company rose for the fourth straight session and currently trade at 8.9 times the average 30-day trading volume, according to Bloomberg. The counter has fallen 7 per cent this year, compared to a 9.8 per cent advance in the benchmark Nifty 50. Siemens has a total market capitalisation of ₹1.12 trillion.

Siemens has reported over 7 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) decline in consolidated net profit to ₹485 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2025. However, the company saw its revenue from operations grow 16 per cent to ₹5,171 crore during the quarter under review from ₹4,457 crore in the year-ago period.

"We delivered a robust performance this quarter, with a surge in revenue, driven by strong performance in our mobility and smart infrastructure businesses, while digital Industries volumes were impacted due to a lower reach in the order backlog from the previous year and muted private sector capex," managing director and chief executive officer, Sunil Mathur, said.

Siemens's topline exceeded estimates by 8 per cent, though the Ebitda beat was a modest 5 per cent due to demerger-related costs, according to JM Financial. The brokerage said profit after tax was ahead of expectations by just 2 per cent, as higher tax outgo and lower other income weighed on the bottom line.
